findings.claim: The enum formatter template has its preprocessor guard inverted: `#if NETSTANDARD2_0 || NETFRAMEWORK`, while every other template uses `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. On modern targets (net6/net8 and others), generated enum formatters are not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. The attribute appears only on the targets the change itself treats as unsupported. This breaks the acceptance criterion that all generated code is decorated.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ReqExcludeFromCodeCoverageGapTests.EnumFormatter_IsExcludedFromCodeCoverage_OnModernTarget. It compiles generated code against net8.0 with no NETSTANDARD2_0/NETFRAMEWORK symbols and asserts that the MyEnum formatter symbol carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. It fails on head. The same applies to EnumTemplate.cs:27.

findings.claim: No generated type gets the attribute when the consuming project targets netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, with class targets allowed. The derived criterion only permits conditional emission where the attribute does not exist, so this exclusion leaves the requirement unmet for those (common) targets.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ReqExcludeFromCodeCoverageGapTests.Formatters_AreExcludedFromCodeCoverage_WhenTargetingNetStandard20. It defines the NETSTANDARD2_0 preprocessor symbol and asserts that the IntKeyed/StringKeyed formatters and the resolver carry the attribute. It fails on head. The same guard appears in StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt, UnionTemplate.tt, ResolverTemplate.tt and CompositeResolverTemplate.tt.

findings.claim: The README states the attribute is 'only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework)'. That is factually wrong: the attribute is available on both. The README also says 'all generated formatters' are decorated, which the inverted enum guard contradicts.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare the netstandard2.0 / net472 reference assemblies, which contain System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute, and EnumTemplate.tt:8, where the guard is inverted.

findings.claim: The resolver attribute is now emitted unconditionally on the generated partial resolver class, and ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class` (an obvious workaround for this very issue) now gets CS0579 (duplicate attribute), and the build breaks on upgrade. With no opt-out setting there is no way around it other than removing the user's attribute.

receipt_plan.detail: Use a VerifyCS.Test with TestBehaviors.SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and a source containing `[System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage][GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class MyResolver {}` plus one [MessagePackObject] type. It passes on base and reports CS0579 on head (net8.0 references). The same applies to CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Always-on, no setting. The templates unconditionally emit [global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on every generated formatter (int-key, string-key, enum, union) and on the generated resolver/composite resolver types and their nested helper classes, guarded only by a TFM #if. This is what the change implements, though the guard is inverted for enums and over-broad for netstandard2.0/.NET Framework.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Same emission, but behind an opt-out setting the requirement explicitly allows. Add a bool option (for example GeneratorOptions/FormattersOptions.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, default true, readable from an MSBuild/analyzer-config property such as build_property.MessagePackExcludeFromCodeCoverage and/or a GeneratedMessagePackResolver attribute argument). Each template wraps its `#if ... [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] #endif` block in `<# if (Options.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage) { #> ... <# } #>`. Users who already decorate their resolver, or who want coverage of generated code, can turn it off, which avoids the CS0579 duplicate-attribute break.
